t: Simplified Fractions — GCD Filtering Over All Pairs
o: We must list every fraction a/b with 1 <= a < b <= n, but only those in lowest terms. A fraction is simplified exactly when gcd(a, b) = 1, so the task reduces to enumerating all pairs and keeping coprime ones. In Example 1 (n = 2), only 1/2 exists and it is already reduced. For n = 3 we check 1/2, 1/3, 2/3 — all have gcd 1, so all are kept. For n = 4, the pair (2,4) has gcd 2, so "2/4" is dropped while the other five pairs survive. With n <= 100 there are at most ~5000 pairs, so even a brute-force double loop with a gcd check per pair is trivially fast; no clever enumeration (like Farey sequences) is required.
k: A fraction a/b is in lowest terms if and only if gcd(a, b) == 1.
Enumerating all O(n^2) numerator-denominator pairs and filtering by gcd is sufficient for n <= 100.
The Euclidean algorithm computes gcd in O(log n), making each pair's check nearly constant time.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with GCD Check
a.i: Loop over every denominator b from 2 to n and every numerator a from 1 to b-1. Keep the pair only when gcd(a, b) equals 1, since that is precisely the definition of a simplified fraction. This directly mirrors the problem definition and needs no extra data structures or deduplication, because each (a, b) pair produces a unique string.
s: For each denominator b from 2 to n:
For each numerator a from 1 to b - 1:
If gcd(a, b) == 1, append the string "a/b" to the result.
a.t: O(n^2 log n) — there are n(n-1)/2 pairs and each gcd via the Euclidean algorithm takes O(log n).
a.sp: O(1) extra space excluding the output list, which holds up to ~n^2/2 strings.

a.n: Approach 2: Sieve-style Deduplication with a Seen Set
a.i: Instead of testing gcd for every pair, generate every fraction a/b and reduce it by dividing both parts by their gcd, then use a set of reduced strings to avoid duplicates. This trades the gcd filter for string hashing; it is equally valid and shows an alternative way to think about uniqueness. It is slightly slower due to set operations but conceptually simple.
s: Create an empty hash set and result list.
For each denominator b from 2 to n and numerator a from 1 to b - 1:
Compute g = gcd(a, b) and form the reduced key (a/g, b/g).
If the key is not in the set, add it and append "a/g + / + b/g" to the result.
a.t: O(n^2 log n) — same pair enumeration plus a gcd per pair; set operations add small constant overhead.
a.sp: O(n^2) for the deduplication set storing up to one entry per generated fraction.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1: it is the optimal practical solution given n <= 100, and stating the gcd(a,b)==1 criterion demonstrates you understand lowest terms. Approach 2 is worth mentioning as an alternative if asked how you would handle duplicates without relying on the gcd property. Common pitfalls: starting the denominator at 1 (which would allow 0/1 or 1/1, both outside the exclusive range), forgetting that a must be strictly less than b, and building strings like "2/4" instead of reducing first when using the set approach. Edge cases: n = 1 returns an empty list since no valid fractions exist. Likely follow-ups: count the fractions instead of listing them (answer is sum over b of Euler's totient phi(b)), generate them in sorted order (Farey sequence generation using the Stern–Brocot recurrence), or handle very large n where an O(n^2) enumeration becomes too slow.
